summary: Documents SLIP, Serial Line IP, a widely used de facto way to carry IP over point-to-point serial connections, since there was no standard for serial lines. The RFC itself says it is not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Before faster connections, home computers used phone cables. SLIP is a simple way to send Internet packets down such a cable, marking where each one ends.

questions: how to send ip over a serial line
what is the maximum slip packet size
what are the limitations of slip
subtitle: A tiny framing trick for sending IP packets down a serial line, documented after it was already in wide use.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP had standard encapsulations for Ethernet, token ring and X.25, but not for plain serial lines, even though people were already running IP over them.
tldr.mechanism: SLIP marks the end of each packet with a special END byte and swaps any END or ESC byte inside the packet for a two-byte escape sequence.
tldr.outcome: SLIP is simple and easy to implement but has no addressing, type field, error checking or compression. The RFC itself calls it a de facto standard, not an Internet standard.

facts.label: Standards status in text
facts.value: De facto, not an Internet standard

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1055 as an Internet Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFCs, although the text itself says SLIP is a de facto standard and not an Internet standard. The RFC notes that successor work was under way to address SLIP's shortcomings.

sections.title: Why SLIP Exists
sections.content:
The TCP/IP family runs over many media, including IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) and 802.5 (token ring) LANs, X.25 lines, satellite links and serial lines. Standard encapsulations existed for many of these, but not for serial lines.

SLIP, Serial Line IP, filled that gap as a de facto standard for point-to-point serial connections running TCP/IP. The RFC states plainly that it is not an Internet standard.
sections.eli5: Computers talking over a plain cable had no official way to package Internet messages. SLIP was the easy way everybody already used.

sections.title: History and Availability
sections.content:
SLIP began in the 3COM UNET TCP/IP implementation of the early 1980's. It is only a packet framing protocol: it defines characters that frame IP packets on a serial line and nothing more. Because it does so little, it is usually very easy to implement.

Around 1984, Rick Adams implemented SLIP for 4.2 Berkeley Unix and Sun Microsystems workstations and released it. It is commonly used on dedicated serial links and sometimes for dialup, usually at line speeds between 1200bps and 19.2Kbps. Host-host, host-router and router-router configurations are all common.

The RFC says SLIP is included in the standard 4.3BSD release and is available for Ultrix, Sun UNIX and most other Berkeley-derived systems. Some terminal concentrators and IBM PC implementations also support it.
sections.eli5: SLIP started in the early 1980s and spread because it was so simple that almost anyone could build it.

sections.title: How SLIP Frames a Packet
sections.content:
SLIP defines two special bytes. END is octal 300 (decimal 192) and ESC is octal 333 (decimal 219). This ESC is not the ASCII ESCape character.

To send a packet, the host simply starts sending its bytes. If a data byte equals END, the two bytes ESC and octal 334 (decimal 220) are sent instead. If a data byte equals ESC, the two bytes ESC and octal 335 (decimal 221) are sent instead. After the last byte, an END is transmitted.

Phil Karn suggested also beginning each packet with an END. This flushes any bytes caused by line noise. Normally the receiver then sees two back-to-back END characters, which produce a zero-length packet that SLIP or IP will discard.

There is no defined maximum packet size. The RFC suggests accepting what the Berkeley UNIX SLIP drivers use: 1006 bytes including IP and transport headers, not counting the framing characters. New implementations should accept 1006 byte datagrams and should not send more than 1006 bytes.
sections.eli5: Each message ends with a stop sign. If the message itself contains something that looks like the stop sign, it is written in a secret two-part code instead, and the receiver turns it back.

sections.title: The Reference C Drivers
sections.content:
The RFC includes C functions that send and receive SLIP packets. They depend on two helpers, send_char() and recv_char(), which move a single character over the serial line.

The sender emits an initial END, replaces each END or ESC data byte with its two-byte sequence, and finishes with a final END. The receiver reads bytes until it sees an END. It ignores an END when nothing has been received yet, to avoid bothering IP with empty packets. It truncates the packet if more than the buffer length arrives.

If ESC is followed by something other than the two defined codes, the receiver treats it as a protocol violation and just stores the byte as it is.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows the recipe in a programming language: add the stop signs, swap the confusing bytes, and on the other side undo it all.

sections.title: Known Deficiencies
sections.content:
The RFC lists commonly perceived shortcomings of SLIP:

  • Addressing: both computers must know each other's IP addresses, and SLIP gives no way to tell a dialing host its address.
  • Type identification: with no type field, only one protocol can run over a SLIP connection, so TCP/IP and DECnet cannot share one line.
  • Error detection and correction: noisy lines corrupt packets and retransmission is expensive at low speeds. IP, UDP and TCP checksums should catch damage, though some applications such as NFS usually ignore the checksum.
  • Compression: dial-in lines are slow, usually 2400bps, and consecutive packets in a TCP connection change few header fields, so sending only the changes could help a lot.

The RFC adds that various groups were working on a successor to address some or all of these problems.
sections.eli5: SLIP is very basic. It does not say who is who, cannot carry different kinds of messages on one cable, cannot fix scrambled messages and does not shrink them.
